name: Glycine
lead: Glycine (Gly, G) is the simplest stable amino acid, with a single hydrogen atom as its side chain, and the only common amino acid that is not chiral. It is a building block of proteins and makes up about 35 percent of the amino acid content of collagen, where its small size allows the tight coiling of the triple helix [1]. It is classed as non-essential because the body synthesises it, though Wikipedia notes it is considered semi-essential because the amount made may not meet all metabolic needs [1].

Beyond its structural role, glycine is an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem, a co-agonist at NMDA glutamate receptors, and a precursor for heme, purines, glutathione and creatine [1][2]. It is inexpensive, available as a sweet-tasting powder supplement, and eaten in gelatin and protein-rich foods.

In recovery and appearance communities glycine is used to support collagen turnover, skin and joints, and sleep. Small human studies and a review by Japanese researchers report that glycine taken before bed improved subjective sleep quality in people with insomniac tendencies [3]. Evidence that supplemental glycine visibly changes skin or connective tissue is indirect: trials of collagen hydrolysates, which are rich in glycine but contain many other amino acids and peptides, are not tests of glycine itself [8].
infobox: Dietary supplement; US FDA no longer regards it as GRAS for human food since 1971 (conditional food use) [1]

paras: Glycine (2-aminoacetic acid) exists mainly as a zwitterion in water and is a white, sweet, crystalline solid [1]. It was discovered in 1820 when Henri Braconnot boiled gelatin with sulfuric acid, initially calling the product 'sugar of gelatin'; Boussingault showed in 1838 that it contained nitrogen, and Berzelius proposed the current name [1]. Industrially it is produced by chemical synthesis rather than isolation from protein, with about 15 thousand tonnes made a year [1].

In the body glycine is made from serine by serine hydroxymethyltransferase and degraded mainly through the glycine cleavage system [1]. It provides the central C2N unit of purines and, with succinyl-CoA, the precursor of porphyrins, and is used to conjugate bile acids and clear sodium benzoate as hippuric acid [1].

Glycine powder is taken before bed to improve sleep, as a collagen-supporting amino acid, and in combinations such as GlyNAC (glycine with N-acetylcysteine) aimed at glutathione and ageing [3][4]. Wikipedia notes that glycine is not widely used in foods for nutrition apart from infusions, and is used in food chemistry mainly as a mild sweetener that counters saccharin aftertaste [1].

In looksmaxxing contexts it is mentioned as part of collagen and recovery routines and in long supplement lists, including peptide and hormone users' daily regimens, but dedicated forum discussion of glycine itself is limited.

Glycine is a component of intravenous amino acid infusions and a laboratory buffer, and glycine-transporter inhibitors have been tested in schizophrenia: a randomised trial of the glycine transporter 1 inhibitor PF-03463275 examined cognitive training and neuroplasticity [9]. Several registered trials test oral glycine in older adults, metabolic syndrome and fatty liver disease [10][11][12].

Glycine activates inhibitory glycine receptors, which are chloride channels abundant in the spinal cord, brainstem and retina, and acts as a required co-agonist with glutamate at NMDA receptors [1][2]. Strychnine is a strong antagonist at the inhibitory receptor [1]. In 2023, researchers reported that the orphan receptor GPR158 acts as a metabotropic glycine receptor [5].

For sleep, researchers propose that oral glycine lowers core body temperature by increasing skin blood flow, a change associated with sleep onset. In rats, oral glycine raised plasma and cerebrospinal fluid glycine, decreased core temperature and increased cutaneous blood flow, and later work found these effects were mediated by NMDA receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus [3][6]. For inflammation, a 2023 review attributes anti-inflammatory effects to modulation of NF-kappa B, though noting the mechanism is not clear [7].
Wikipedia reports that the half-life of glycine and its elimination vary significantly with dose [1].

Sleep: A review in the Journal of Pharmacological Sciences reported that glycine ingestion before bedtime significantly improved subjective sleep quality in people with insomniac tendencies, alongside rat data on body temperature [3]. The review describes the human findings as the authors' own recent reports, and no larger independent confirmation is described there [3].

Ageing and metabolism: A 2023 review describes glycine as extending lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice and rats and improving health in animal models of age-related disease, with proposed involvement of glycine N-methyltransferase and methionine clearance, while stating that mechanisms may be divergent [13]. A 2023 randomised trial in older adults tested GlyNAC, glycine combined with N-acetylcysteine, and reported improvements in glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation and physical function [4]; because it used a combination, it does not isolate the effect of glycine. A 2016 meta-analysis of metabolomics studies found higher glycine concentrations among other amino acids in people with type 2 diabetes versus controls, which is an association study, not a supplementation trial [14].

Exercise and recovery: A 2024 update reviews the promise of glycine supplementation for physical performance and recovery [15]. A review of glycine as a multifunctional non-essential amino acid collects reported benefits in animal and human studies [16].

Skin: A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of bioactive collagen hydrolysates reported improved facial skin moisture and elasticity and reduced signs of facial ageing [8]; collagen hydrolysate is a mixture of peptides, so this is not evidence for free glycine itself. No trial of glycine alone for skin appearance was identified.

Human data on glycine supplementation are limited and mostly for non-cosmetic outcomes. The sleep trials are described in a 2012 review [3]; the GlyNAC trial in older adults is a combination study [4]; and a trial of a glycine transporter inhibitor addressed schizophrenia rather than glycine supplementation [9]. Registered studies include dietary glycine for cognitive performance in older adults with insulin resistance (NCT07643675, n=59, completed) [10], a phase 2/3 trial of glycine for atherosclerosis and metabolic syndrome parameters (NCT03850314, n=50) [11], dietary glycine in metabolic-dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (NCT07285135, n=90, recruiting) [12], and a terminated trial of glycine supplement for severe COVID-19 (NCT04443673, n=59) [17].
No studies of oral glycine for skin, hair or facial appearance outcomes were found.

Glycine is a normal dietary and body constituent. In the 1970s the US FDA stopped regarding glycine and its salts as generally recognised as safe for human food, allowing food uses under certain conditions, according to Wikipedia [1]. Loss of glycinergic inhibition causes severe disease: tetanus toxin blocks glycine release causing spastic paralysis, and glycine-receptor antibodies are associated with stiff-person syndrome and progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus [1][18]. These are disease states rather than effects of supplementation.

Glycine was found in 1820, named from the Greek for sweet, and shown in 1858 by Auguste Cahours to be an amine of acetic acid [1]. In 1971 its status as a food additive was restricted by the US FDA [1]. Glycine has been detected in space: in the Murchison meteorite in 1970, in samples of comet Wild 2 returned by NASA's Stardust mission (confirmed in 2009) and in comet 67P by Rosetta (announced 2016) [1].

Research on glycine and sleep, including the work summarised in the 2012 review, appeared in the 2000s and 2010s, and work on glycine and longevity expanded in the 2020s after reports of lifespan extension in mice [3][13].

Glycine is cheap and legal as a supplement, and is marketed for sleep, collagen support and longevity. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, provides a similar overview of its roles [19]. Forum discussion in the sources reviewed treated glycine as one item in extensive supplement regimens and not as a subject of dedicated debate.

Cahours identifies glycine as an amine of acetic acid. [1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, glycine is discussed as an inexpensive supplement for collagen, hair, nails and skin, and as a sweet-tasting substitute for sugar [20].

claims.claim: Glycine improves hair, nails and skin because it is needed for collagen synthesis
claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide says glycine improves the nervous system, hair, nails and skin and is necessary for collagen synthesis, and that looksmaxers should be most interested in the collagen and hair effects [20].
claims.experts: Glycine makes up about 35 percent of the amino acids in collagen, but evidence that supplemental glycine visibly changes skin or connective tissue is indirect: trials of collagen hydrolysates are not tests of glycine itself [1][8].

claims.claim: Glycine can replace dietary sugar because it tastes sweet
claims.believers: The guide's author proposes substituting sucrose, fructose and dextrose with glycine, which has a sugary taste. A reply states that glycine is supplemented in amounts of a few grams at most and cannot replace sugar [20].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes glycine is a sweet-tasting solid and is used as a food additive and dietary supplement; the sources cited here do not report trials of glycine as a sugar replacement [1].

claims.claim: Glycine adds a small increase in looks rating (0.05 to 0.2 PSL)
claims.believers: The guide's author estimates a potential 0.05 to 0.2 PSL increase depending on the individual [20].
claims.experts: No published studies in the sources reviewed have tested glycine for facial appearance; small human studies report improved subjective sleep quality with bedtime glycine [3].

claims.claim: Glycine is better taken as collagen powder because amino acids compete for absorption
claims.believers: A reply in the guide thread says small amounts are helpful for cancer and longevity and that taking glycine from collagen powder is better because amino acids compete to be absorbed [20].
claims.experts: Reviews describe glycine in aging and metabolism research, and a trial of collagen hydrolysates reported changes in facial skin moisture; the sources cited here do not compare absorption of free glycine and collagen powder [13][8].
